archetype.name: Playoff Team (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A Bengals team carried by a top-three passing offense, with a league-average defense that gives up yards and third downs but finishes drives well enough to protect the lead the offense builds.

report.headline: Burrow's passing game is elite again; the defense is just good enough.
report.take:
Cincinnati is 6-2 and tied with Pittsburgh atop the AFC North a year after going 6-11. The turnaround is mostly real. The Bengals score 30 points a game (2nd), their point differential per game is 3rd, and their net EPA is 4th. Very little of the record is borrowed: wins over expected sit at 0.92, and the point differential alone implies about five wins. This is a good team that has also been a bit fortunate, not a lucky one.

The engine is Joe Burrow throwing the ball. Cincinnati's pass EPA is 0.262, 2nd in the league, and no team passes more than expected in neutral situations. That isn't a game-script accident; the staff has chosen to put the game in Burrow's hands. Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins split the targets almost evenly, and Chase Brown adds a receiving outlet. The first two weeks were sluggish, with negative passing EPA in both. From Week 3 on, the passing EPA has been positive every week and mostly in the teens. The run game adds almost nothing: rush EPA is 17th and backs get only 2.18 yards before contact (26th). The offense runs the ball to stay balanced, not to move it.

The defense is the part to read carefully. After ranking 29th in EPA allowed in 2025, it is now 16th, and the improvement shows up where it matters most. Cincinnati is 6th in pressure rate, 5th in takeaways and 5th in red-zone touchdown rate allowed, and it is 4th against deep passes. The rest of the profile is worse. It ranks 27th in rush EPA allowed, 30th on third downs and 25th against short passes, and yards allowed per game rank 26th. Opponents move the ball, convert, and then stall near the goal line or give it away. That bend-don't-break pattern props up the points-allowed figure more than the underlying play does.

That sets the ceiling. With this passing game the Bengals can beat anyone in a shootout, as they did against Tennessee, 43-36. Against a team that can run the ball and shorten the game, the defense's leaks on early downs and third downs become the story. Pittsburgh, the team that beat them in Week 3, is built to do exactly that.

strengths.title: Top-two passing offense, by design
strengths.body: Cincinnati ranks 2nd in pass EPA and 1st in pass rate over expected. The staff leans on Burrow, Chase and Higgins in every situation, not just when trailing. Since a slow first two weeks the passing game has been consistently strong, and with the same quarterback starting every week there is little reason to expect a drop-off.

strengths.title: Defense finishes drives and takes the ball
strengths.body: Opponents gain yards, but the Bengals rank 5th in red-zone touchdown rate allowed and 5th in takeaways. That limits the damage of a defense that otherwise ranks 16th in EPA allowed. Turnovers and red-zone stops are among the least stable defensive traits, so expect some of this to fade.

strengths.title: Pass rush and deep coverage hold up
strengths.body: A 25.3% pressure rate (6th) pairs with the 4th-best EPA against deep throws. Quarterbacks rarely get the time or the space to beat this secondary over the top. Pressure tends to be a stickier skill than takeaways, though losing Cashius Howell to IR thins the edge rotation into December.

concerns.title: Run defense and third downs leak
concerns.body: The Bengals rank 27th in rush EPA allowed and 30th in third-down rate allowed. The deep coverage is sound, but the defense keeps giving up underneath completions (25th in short-pass EPA) and ground gains, which keeps drives alive. Tennessee and Atlanta both ran for more than 150 yards in recent weeks. This looks like a real flaw rather than a sample quirk.

concerns.title: No run game, shaky protection
concerns.body: Backs get little room: 2.18 yards before contact ranks 26th, and rush EPA is 17th. Burrow holds the ball longer than almost anyone (29th in time to throw), behind a line that ranks 23rd in pressure rate allowed. The sack rate is fine because Burrow escapes, but a good pass rush can still make the offense one-dimensional and hurried.

concerns.title: Turnovers in high-volume games
concerns.body: The offense has turned it over 10 times, including four in the Tennessee shootout and two in each of the losses. It is the cost of throwing this much. The defense's takeaways have covered for it so far, but if those regress, the giveaways start costing games.

trend.note: The passing offense went from negative EPA in Weeks 1-2 to strong weekly totals ever since, and the Bengals have won four straight. The defense has gone the other way against the run lately, giving up big rushing totals to Tennessee and Atlanta.

nextGame.headline: Rematch with Pittsburgh pits Burrow's arm against the league's best run game
nextGame.body:
This is a first-place rematch at home, with the Bengals favored by 3.5 after losing 30-27 in Pittsburgh in Week 3. The styles are opposite. Pittsburgh has the league's best rushing offense by EPA, a passing attack that ranks 26th, and a defense that is 6th in EPA allowed and 3rd in sacks. Cincinnati has the elite pass offense and the leaky run defense. The Steelers' defense is stingy underneath and against opposing WR1s, but it ranks 23rd against deep passes, which is where Burrow can punish it. Pittsburgh's 6-2 record also leans on close-game results: it is 3rd in one-score win rate and its wins over expected are higher than Cincinnati's.

For Cincinnati, tight end Erick All Jr. is done for the season, Cashius Howell is on IR (39% of snaps), and safety Kyle Dugger (a part-timer) is out. Andrei Iosivas may come off IR around this date, but nothing is confirmed. Pittsburgh may be without WR Michael Pittman Jr. (78% of snaps), who has no clear activation timeline, which makes its weak passing game thinner still. It is also missing DT Sebastian Joseph-Day and depth corners Brandin Echols and Doneiko Slaughter, which could matter when Cincinnati spreads it out with three receivers.

waysToWin.title: Win over the top
waysToWin.body: Pittsburgh's defense is good underneath and on early downs but ranks 23rd in EPA allowed on deep throws. With Chase and Higgins and the league's most pass-heavy approach, Cincinnati can go after those shots and score quickly, without needing long drives against a strong third-down defense.

waysToWin.title: Make Rodgers beat them throwing
waysToWin.body: Pittsburgh's pass offense ranks 26th by EPA, and its line ranks 21st in sack rate. If Cincinnati gets an early lead, the Steelers have to throw into a pass rush ranked 6th in pressure rate, and they may be without Pittman.

waysToWin.title: Special teams and the tight end
waysToWin.body: Cincinnati's special teams rank 9th by EPA per game, while Pittsburgh's rank 23rd, so field position could tilt the Bengals' way. Pittsburgh is also 30th in EPA allowed to tight ends, which gives Mike Gesicki room to work with All gone.

waysToLose.title: Steelers run and keep the ball
waysToLose.body: Pittsburgh's rushing offense is 1st in EPA and 2nd in yards per carry, and it faces a run defense ranked 27th that struggles on third downs. The Steelers ran for 138 yards in the first meeting. If they control the clock, Burrow gets fewer possessions against a defense that ranks 7th on third downs and 3rd in the red zone.

waysToLose.title: Pass rush gets to Burrow
waysToLose.body: Pittsburgh is 3rd in sacks and 4th in sack rate. Cincinnati's line ranks 23rd in pressure rate allowed, and Burrow holds the ball longer than almost anyone. With no run game to slow the rush, drive-killing sacks and hurried turnovers are the most likely way the offense stalls.

waysToLose.title: A one-score game slips away
waysToLose.body: Pittsburgh has been one of the league's best closers, with a 0.8 one-score win rate (3rd), and it commits very few penalties. If turnovers keep this close the way they did in Week 3, the Steelers' pattern of winning tight games is a real threat, whether or not it holds up over time.

nextGame.watch: Pittsburgh's early-down rushing success: if Cincinnati's 27th-ranked run defense holds up on first and second down, the Steelers are forced into passing downs they can't handle.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the sustainable part. It is built on Burrow's passing efficiency, a quarterback who has started every week, and a target tree split between two top receivers. Expect it to keep scoring near the top of the league, maybe a bit below 30 a game as opponents improve. The defense is harder to trust. Its pressure is real, but the red-zone stops and takeaways are flattering a unit that gives up yards and third downs. Points allowed will probably creep up somewhat rather than fall.

The schedule helps. After Pittsburgh, only Kansas City looks like a top opponent. Washington, New Orleans, Carolina and Indianapolis all have losing records, and the two Cleveland games plus a Baltimore rematch fill out the division slate. A modest dose of luck so far means slight regression, not a collapse. The division likely comes down to this week and whether Pittsburgh's close-game magic holds.
swingFactors: Result of the Pittsburgh rematch for the division
Run defense against physical rushing teams
Takeaway and red-zone luck holding up

confidence.note: Eight games with a stable quarterback; defensive gains lean on volatile red-zone and turnover numbers.
